name: Spur gear pair
summary: Two involute gears on parallel shafts turn in opposite directions at a fixed speed ratio set by their tooth counts.

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one gear mesh higher pair

explain.motion: The 14-tooth pinion drives the 28-tooth gear, so the gear turns half as fast and the other way. Involute teeth roll and slide against each other so that the speed ratio stays exactly constant at every instant of the mesh, not just on average.
explain.forces: Tooth contact always lies on the line of action, tilted by the 20° pressure angle from the common tangent of the pitch circles. The tangential part turns the gear while the radial part pushes the shafts apart into the bearings; halving the speed doubles the torque, less about 1 to 2% friction.
explain.benefits: Constant velocity ratio, about 98% efficiency, simple to make and inspect, and the ratio is exact because it is counted in teeth. Involute teeth tolerate small centre-distance errors without changing the ratio.
explain.limits: Teeth engage across the full face at once, so spur gears are noisier than helical gears at speed. Ratios above about 6:1 in one pair need a tiny pinion that suffers undercut (below 17 teeth at 20° without profile shift).

build.ground: frame carrying both shaft bearings at a fixed centre distance
build.output: gear, rotation angle th2 about O2

name: Compound gear train
summary: Two gear pairs stacked on a shared middle shaft multiply their ratios, giving 3 x 3 = 9:1 in a compact space.

ratio.typical: product of stage ratios, e.g. 3 x 3 = 9:1; 2 stages give up to about 40:1

topology.notes: ground, input pinion a, cluster b+c (one rigid body), output gear d; two gear meshes

explain.motion: A 12-tooth input pinion drives a 36-tooth gear three times slower. A second 12-tooth pinion fixed to that same shaft, one layer up, drives a final 36-tooth gear another three times slower, so the output turns once for every nine input turns, in the same direction as the input.
explain.forces: Torque grows stage by stage: about 3x on the cluster shaft and 9x on the output, so the last mesh carries the highest tooth load and usually needs the widest face. Each mesh loses 1 to 2% to friction, so efficiency is the product of stage efficiencies.
explain.benefits: A single 9:1 pair would need a gear nine times the pinion size; compounding reaches the same ratio with small gears, and every extra stage multiplies the ratio again.
explain.limits: More stages add backlash, inertia and parts. Direction depends on the number of external meshes, and high ratios are usually more compact as planetary or worm drives.

name: Internal gear pair
summary: A pinion meshes inside a ring with teeth on its inner rim, so both turn the same way on close, parallel shafts.

topology.notes: ground, pinion, internal gear; one internal gear mesh

explain.motion: The 18-tooth pinion rolls inside a 40-tooth internal gear. Because the teeth meet on the same side of both centres, ring and pinion turn in the same direction, the ring at 18/40 of the pinion speed.
explain.forces: A concave ring tooth wraps around a convex pinion tooth, so contact stress is lower and more teeth share the load than in an external pair. The radial separating force acts toward the ring centre and is taken by both bearings.
explain.benefits: Very short centre distance (half the tooth-count difference times the module), same-direction rotation without an idler, and a natural housing for planetary sets.
explain.limits: Too small a tooth difference causes tip and trochoid interference, so standard 20° gears need about 10 or more teeth difference and more than 34 ring teeth. Internal teeth must be shaped or broached rather than hobbed, which costs more.

name: Helical gear pair
summary: Gears with teeth cut on a helix engage gradually, running quieter and stronger than spur gears but pushing their shafts axially.

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one helical gear mesh (line contact sweeps diagonally across the face)

explain.motion: Seen end-on, a helical pair behaves exactly like a spur pair: the 17-tooth pinion drives the 34-tooth gear at half speed in the opposite direction. Along the face the teeth are twisted at 20°, so each tooth comes into contact at one end and the contact line sweeps across, with several teeth always sharing load.
explain.forces: The tooth force has a tangential part that does the work, a radial part, and an axial thrust equal to tangential force times tan(helix angle), here about 36% of it. That thrust must be taken by thrust-capable bearings, and the two gears must have opposite hands.
explain.benefits: Gradual engagement and a higher total contact ratio give much quieter running and higher load capacity than spur gears of the same size, which is why nearly all car gearboxes use them.
explain.limits: Axial thrust needs angular-contact or tapered bearings, and extra sliding lowers efficiency slightly. Gears cannot be slid in and out of mesh as easily as spur gears.

name: Herringbone gear pair
summary: Two opposite-hand helical halves side by side cancel each other's axial thrust, giving smooth, heavy-duty parallel-shaft drive.

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one double-helical mesh; one shaft usually allowed to float axially

explain.motion: Each gear is two helical gears of opposite hand joined face to face, forming a V of teeth. End-on it behaves like a spur pair, while along the face both halves engage gradually and many teeth share the load.
explain.forces: The axial thrust of the left half (Ft/2 x tan beta) is equal and opposite to that of the right half, so they cancel and only radial bearings are needed. One shaft is left free to float axially so the two halves share load equally.
explain.benefits: Allows large helix angles (25° to 45°) for very smooth, high-capacity drive without thrust bearings; historically key to marine steam turbine reduction gears.
explain.limits: Hard to manufacture accurately (needs a central relief groove or a Sykes-type shaper), and a mismatch between halves overloads one side. More expensive than single helical gears.

name: Bevel gear pair
summary: Cone-shaped gears transmit rotation between intersecting shafts, usually at a right angle, with a fixed ratio.

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one bevel mesh; pitch cones share an apex at the shaft intersection

explain.motion: Two toothed cones roll on each other with a common apex where the shafts cross. The 16-tooth pinion turns the 32-tooth gear at half speed about an axis at 90°, and the pitch cone angles (26.6° and 63.4°) are set by the tooth ratio.
explain.forces: Tooth force splits into tangential, radial and axial parts; both gears are pushed away from the cone apex along their own axes, so each shaft needs a thrust-capable bearing. Load is concentrated toward the large end of the tooth.
explain.benefits: The simplest way to turn a drive through a corner with an exact ratio and high efficiency (about 97 to 98%).
explain.limits: Mounting must be precise because both apexes must coincide; errors shift the contact patch and cause noise or tooth breakage. Straight bevels are noisy at speed, so spiral bevels are used there.

name: Hypoid gear pair
summary: A spiral bevel pair with the pinion axis offset below the gear centre, so the shafts cross without meeting; used in car rear axles.

ratio.typical: 2.5:1 to 5:1 in car axles, up to about 10:1; default 41/10 = 4.1:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, ring gear; one hypoid mesh with sliding along the tooth

explain.motion: The 10-tooth pinion drives a 41-tooth ring gear through 90°, but its axis passes 25 mm below the ring gear centre. To mesh at that offset the pinion has a larger spiral angle than the gear, which makes it larger and stronger than a spiral bevel pinion of the same ratio.
explain.forces: The offset adds sliding along the teeth, so tooth friction is higher than in a bevel pair and extreme-pressure hypoid oil is required. Contact is spread over several curved teeth at once, giving high load capacity and smooth, quiet running.
explain.benefits: The lowered pinion lets a car's propeller shaft sit lower (less floor tunnel), and the bigger pinion and higher contact ratio carry more torque quietly.
explain.limits: Efficiency (about 90 to 96%) is lower than bevel gears, requires special lubricant, and setup of pinion depth and backlash is critical. Manufacturing needs dedicated Gleason or Klingelnberg type machines.

name: Worm drive
summary: A screw-like worm turns a toothed wheel on a crossing shaft, giving a large reduction in one stage that often cannot be driven backwards.

ratio.typical: 5:1 to 75:1 per stage (up to about 100:1); ratio = wheel teeth / worm starts; default 30:1

topology.notes: ground, worm, wheel; one worm mesh (screw-type sliding contact)

explain.motion: The worm is a screw with one thread (start). Each worm turn advances the wheel by one tooth, so a 30-tooth wheel turns once per 30 worm turns. The shafts cross at 90° without intersecting.
explain.forces: Contact is mostly sliding along the thread, so friction is high and efficiency falls from about 90% at low ratios to under 50% at high ratios. With a small lead angle (here 5.7°) friction exceeds the driving component when the wheel tries to turn the worm, so the drive locks.
explain.benefits: Very high reduction in one compact, quiet stage, and a self-locking worm holds loads without a brake in many uses.
explain.limits: Low efficiency and heat build-up; a steel worm needs a bronze wheel and good lubrication. Self-locking is unreliable under vibration, so it should not replace a safety brake on hoists.

name: Crossed helical gears
summary: Two helical gears on non-parallel, non-intersecting shafts touch at a point and drive each other, usually at 90°, for light loads.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to about 5:1; ratio = z2/z1 (not pitch diameter ratio); default 24/12 = 2:1

topology.notes: ground, gear 1, gear 2; one point-contact crossed helical mesh

explain.motion: Two ordinary helical gears of the same hand are mounted on shafts crossing at 90° at a set distance. With 45° helix angles the teeth line up and gear 1 (12 teeth) turns gear 2 (24 teeth) at half speed.
explain.forces: Contact is a single point that slides along the teeth, so load capacity is low and wear is high. Each gear sees an axial thrust that must be taken by its bearings.
explain.benefits: Lets two standard helical gears drive between skew shafts, and centre distance and ratio can be tuned by choosing different helix angles. Insensitive to small centre-distance errors.
explain.limits: Point contact and high sliding limit them to light power, such as camshaft-driven distributors and oil pumps; for real loads use a worm or hypoid set.

name: Rack and pinion
summary: A gear meshing with a straight toothed bar: every turn of the pinion moves the rack one pitch-circle circumference.

ratio.typical: travel = pitch radius x angle; 100.5 mm per pinion turn at m = 4, z = 16

topology.notes: ground, pinion, rack; rack slides in a guide; one gear mesh

explain.motion: The pinion swings back and forth and the rack slides with it. The rack moves exactly the pinion's pitch radius times the angle turned, so travel is proportional to rotation in both directions.
explain.forces: Torque on the pinion becomes a straight push on the rack equal to torque divided by pitch radius. The 20° pressure angle adds a force pushing rack and pinion apart, which the rack guide or a backing roller must resist so the teeth cannot climb out.
explain.benefits: Simple, stiff and reversible; long strokes only need a longer rack, and several pinions can share one rack.
explain.limits: Backlash makes precise reversal hard without preloaded or split pinions, and long racks need accurate joining and straight guides.

name: Planetary gear set
summary: Planets orbit a central sun inside a ring gear; hold the ring, drive the sun, and the carrier turns slowly in line with the input.

ratio.typical: 3:1 to 10:1 per stage with ring fixed; default 1 + 35/13 = 3.69:1

topology.notes: ground+ring (fixed), sun, carrier, 3 planets; sun and carrier revolute to ground, each planet revolute on carrier; 3 sun-planet and 3 planet-ring meshes (redundant planets). Kinematic mobility 2 with ring free, 1 with ring fixed

explain.motion: The sun drives three planets, which roll around inside the fixed ring and carry the carrier with them. With 13 sun teeth and a 35-tooth ring, the carrier turns once for every 1 + 35/13 = 3.69 turns of the sun, in the same direction, while each planet spins backwards on its own pin.
explain.forces: Load is shared between three planets, so each mesh carries about a third of the torque and the radial pushes on the sun cancel. The ring reacts the difference between input and output torque.
explain.benefits: Coaxial input and output, very high torque density, and by choosing which of sun, ring or carrier is held, the same parts give different ratios; with two inputs it adds or subtracts speeds.
explain.limits: Tooth counts are constrained by assembly and spacing rules, load sharing needs accurate parts or floating members, and the many meshes make it costlier than a simple pair.

name: Differential
summary: Splits one input between two output shafts so they can turn at different speeds, their average always equal to the carrier speed.

ratio.typical: final drive 2.5:1 to 5:1 into the case; 1:1 average to the two side shafts; default 41/10 = 4.1:1

topology.notes: ground, input pinion, ring gear+case (carrier), left side gear, right side gear, spider pinions (2, counted as 1 body type); meshes: pinion-ring, 2 spiders x 2 side gears. Mobility 2: case speed and wheel speed difference

explain.motion: The input pinion turns the ring gear and the case it is bolted to. Spider pinions on a cross-pin in the case drive two side gears; when the car goes straight the spiders do not spin and both wheels turn with the case, and in a turn the spiders spin so the outer wheel speeds up as much as the inner slows down.
explain.forces: An open differential always gives equal torque to both outputs, so the wheel with least grip limits total traction. The spider pinions only carry load across their own teeth and turn only when the wheels differ in speed.
explain.benefits: Lets driven wheels on one axle cover different distances in a turn without scrubbing tyres, and as a mechanism it adds or averages two rotations exactly.
explain.limits: If one wheel loses grip it spins and the other gets almost no torque; limited-slip or locking differentials address this at the cost of complexity.

name: Harmonic drive
summary: An elliptical wave generator flexes a thin toothed cup inside a rigid ring with two more teeth, giving a 50:1 to 160:1 coaxial reduction with no backlash.

ratio.typical: 30:1 to 160:1 per stage; ratio = Zf / (Zc - Zf); default 100/2 = 50:1

topology.notes: ground with circular spline, wave generator, flexspline (compliant), plus the wave generator bearing rolling on the flexspline; one multi-tooth mesh at two zones

explain.motion: An elliptical cam with a thin ball bearing (the wave generator) spins inside a flexible cup with 100 external teeth (the flexspline), bending it so its teeth engage a rigid 102-tooth ring at the two ends of the long axis. Each wave generator turn shifts the flexspline back by two teeth relative to the ring, so the flexspline turns once, backwards, per 50 input turns.
explain.forces: About 30% of the teeth are in contact at once, giving high torque capacity and stiffness for the size. The flexspline is cyclically bent every half turn, so its fatigue strength sets the torque and life limits.
explain.benefits: High single-stage ratio, near-zero backlash, coaxial hollow-shaft design and light weight make it the standard robot joint reducer.
explain.limits: Torsional compliance is higher than in rigid gears, the flexspline can fail by fatigue or ratcheting under overload, and efficiency falls at high ratios and low temperatures.

name: Cycloidal drive
summary: An eccentric drives a lobed disc around a ring of pins; one fewer lobe than pins gives a large, compact, shock-tolerant reduction.

ratio.typical: 10:1 to about 100:1 per stage; ratio = n / (N - n); default 11:1

topology.notes: ground with ring pins, eccentric input shaft, cycloidal disc, output flange with pins; higher pairs: disc lobes on ring pins (rolling), output pins in disc holes (pin-in-hole)

explain.motion: The input shaft carries an eccentric that makes the cycloidal disc wobble around inside a ring of 12 fixed pins. Because the disc has 11 lobes, one fewer than the pins, it rolls backwards by one lobe for every input turn, and pins on the output flange running in holes in the disc pick off that slow rotation.
explain.forces: Many lobes touch ring pins at once (in theory about half), so load is shared and the drive survives shock loads well. The eccentric disc creates an unbalanced force, so real units use two discs 180° apart.
explain.benefits: High ratio in one compact stage, rolling contact with high efficiency (often above 90%), high shock tolerance and low backlash.
explain.limits: Single discs vibrate unless balanced, the profile must be made precisely, and output torque has a small ripple. More parts than a planetary stage.

name: Non-circular gears
summary: Gears with non-round pitch curves, such as a pair of ellipses turning on their foci, give a speed ratio that varies through each turn.

ratio.typical: ratio swings between (1-e)/(1+e) and (1+e)/(1-e) each turn; 0.54 to 1.86 at e = 0.3

topology.notes: ground, gear 1, gear 2; one non-circular gear mesh

explain.motion: Two identical elliptical gears each turn about one focus, with the foci 80 mm apart (the major axis length). As the driver turns steadily, the contact point moves along the ellipses, so the driven gear speeds up and slows down once per turn, from 0.54 to 1.86 times the input speed.
explain.forces: Torque transmitted scales inversely with the instantaneous speed ratio, so the driven shaft sees cyclic torque and the system sees inertia loads from the varying speed. Pressure angle varies along the profile, which limits the eccentricity before teeth jam or undercut.
explain.benefits: Produces an exact, repeatable non-uniform motion with continuous rotation, useful for quick-return strokes, matching cutter speed to web speed, or oval-gear flow metering.
explain.limits: Hard to design and manufacture (each tooth differs), noisier than round gears, and large eccentricity causes undercut and interference. Cams or linkages are often cheaper for one-off motion laws.

build.input: gear 1, continuous rotation about focus F1
